309.title: "Recitation": the name
309.hook: the word means recitation: it was spoken before it was written
309.howItsDone: Muslims learn the Qur'an first by listening and repeating after a teacher, and recite it aloud in prayer, in Ramadan and at home; some say it is fully itself only when it is recited.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the heart's polish: the heart as a mirror, and remembrance as the cloth. Your line was polish the heart. Did you wipe one film away? That closed the Sufi path. Today a new strand begins. Day three hundred nine.

A parent at bedtime, doing all the voices. A friend reading a message out loud, in a funny accent. Words change when someone says them. They get a speed, a breath, a face behind them. Now: the book at the center of Islam. Its name is easy to say, and its meaning is easy to miss. That name isn't a word for something written. It's a word for something spoken. For the next three weeks, we look at how the Qur'an is built: its parts, its verses, its scribes and its reciters. Today, the name itself.
screen: `WORDS SOUND DIFFERENT IN A VOICE.` → `WHAT DOES THE NAME MEAN?` → `HOW THE QUR'AN IS BUILT.`

segments.voice: The word Qur'an comes from the Arabic root q, r, and a catch in the throat, which means to read aloud, to recite. Qur'an is recitation, or the thing that is recited. You've met this root before. The first word the angel Jibril brought to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the cave of Hira came from it: iqra'. In Pickthall's words: "Read: In the name of thy Lord who createth." Read and recite are one word in Arabic. And that first revelation came, Muslims say, to a man who did not read or write. So from the very beginning, the Qur'an was heard before it was written. The Prophet recited what came to him. Companions heard it, repeated it and learned it by heart. Scribes wrote it down too, on whatever was at hand, but the living copy was in voices. The hadith collections say that every Ramadan, Jibril went over the Qur'an with the Prophet, recitation for recitation, and in his last year, twice. The Qur'an even tells him how: "chant the Qur'an in measured measure," in Pickthall's rendering of Surah 73. That's why a child's Qur'an lesson traditionally begins with listening to a teacher and repeating, not with silent reading. It's why the prayer, the call to prayer and the nights of Ramadan are full of recitation. The Qur'an also calls itself kitab, a writing, and Muslims hold both: a book you can hold, and a voice you can hear. But its own name leans toward the voice. When people say it doesn't feel the same on a silent page, this is part of what they mean. It was made to be said.
screen: `FROM THE ROOT: TO RECITE` · `IQRA': THE FIRST WORD` · `HEARD BEFORE IT WAS WRITTEN` · `A BOOK AND A VOICE`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recite something aloud. If you know al-Fatiha, or any short surah from the juz' you walked through, say it now, out loud, not in your head. Slowly. Hear what your voice does with it. If you're learning, say the one line you know best, even just bismillah, or read a line of anything you love at a speaking pace. Then sit in the quiet after it, and notice the words still hanging in the room. The bell holds the time.
Qur'an. Recitation: the thing that is recited, from the same root as iqra', read. Today's word.

Your line: the book is a voice. Today, read one thing aloud that you'd normally read silently, a verse, a poem, a message from someone you love, and notice what the voice adds. Day three hundred nine.

310.title: Twenty-three years
310.hook: it came in parts over about twenty-three years, as situations arose (17:106)
310.howItsDone: Muslims teach that the Qur'an was revealed in parts over about twenty-three years, and students of the Qur'an learn the occasions of revelation (asbab al-nuzul) for many verses to understand them in their setting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Qur'an: recitation, a voice before a page. Your line was the book is a voice. Did you read something aloud, and did it change? Day three hundred ten.

A letter arrives one paragraph at a time, over twenty-three years. Some paragraphs come when you're frightened. Some come the week you lose someone. Some come while your town is arguing about what's fair. Each one answers something happening right then, and together they make one letter. That's how Muslims describe the Qur'an arriving: not handed down as a finished book in a single night, but in parts, over about twenty-three years, from the cave of Hira to the last months of the Prophet's life. Today: twenty-three years.
screen: `A LETTER, ONE PARAGRAPH AT A TIME.` → `EACH ONE ANSWERS A MOMENT.` → `FROM THE CAVE TO THE LAST MONTHS.`

segments.voice: A report from Ibn Abbas in al-Bukhari gives the span: revelation began when the Prophet ﷺ was forty, and he lived thirteen years in Mecca, then ten in Medina, until he died. In between, verses arrived as situations arose: a question someone asked, a hardship, a dispute, a battle, a grief. The Qur'an says so itself. In Pickthall's words: "And (it is) a Qur'an that We have divided, that thou mayst recite it unto mankind at intervals, and We have revealed it by (successive) revelation." Another verse records people asking why it wasn't sent down all at once, and answers: so that the Prophet's heart would be made firm by it. Muslim scholars add a detail. A report from Ibn Abbas says the Qur'an came down whole to the nearest heaven on the Night of Power, and from there to the Prophet in parts. So Muslims speak of both: complete, and arriving slowly. And there's a reason people often give: gentleness. Aisha, the Prophet's wife, said the first things revealed were short surahs about paradise and the fire, and only once people's hearts had turned did the rules on what's allowed and forbidden come. If the first thing revealed had been do not drink wine, she said, people would have answered: we will never give it up. Scholars call the stories behind particular verses asbab al-nuzul, the occasions of revelation. A woman named Khawlah came to the Prophet about her husband's harsh treatment and argued her case, and the opening of Surah 58 came about her: Allah has heard the one who pleads with you. Not every verse has a known occasion, and scholars weigh those reports carefully. But the picture holds: a book that met people where they were, one piece at a time.
screen: `FROM THE CAVE TO HIS LAST YEAR` · `DIVIDED, TO RECITE AT INTERVALS` · `GENTLENESS FIRST, RULES LATER` · `THE OCCASIONS OF REVELATION`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one verse's occasion, and hold it. Picture Khawlah: a woman with trouble at home, going to the Prophet, pleading her case, and being heard. The verse opens by saying her voice reached Allah. Now bring to mind one situation in your own life that you'd want answered. Don't solve it. Just hold it, the way she carried hers in. If you pray, you can bring it to Allah in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Twenty-three years. How long the Qur'an took to arrive: in parts, from the cave of Hira to the Prophet's last year, as life happened. Today's word.
Your line: it came slowly. Today, when something good in you is growing slowly, a habit, a skill, a healing, let it be slow, and take the one piece in front of you. Day three hundred ten.

311.title: One hundred and fourteen
311.hook: 114 surahs, arranged mostly longest to shortest, not by date
311.howItsDone: Muslims know the surahs by name and number; children usually learn them from the short end of the book first, and a printed mushaf lists all 114 with their names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, twenty-three years: the Qur'an arriving in parts, as life happened. Your line was it came slowly. Did you let one thing be slow? Day three hundred eleven.

Open a mushaf for the first time and you might expect it to start where the story starts: the cave, the angel, the first word, iqra'. It doesn't. That first word is near the very back, in Surah 96. The book opens with al-Fatiha, seven short verses, and then comes the longest surah of all, al-Baqarah. From there the surahs get shorter, more or less, until the tiny ones at the end that you walked through in camp four. Today: one hundred and fourteen.
screen: `THE FIRST WORD IS NEAR THE BACK.` → `IT OPENS WITH AL-FATIHA.` → `ONE HUNDRED AND FOURTEEN.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an has one hundred and fourteen surahs, or chapters. Scholars aren't certain where the word surah comes from. Some connect it to sur, a city wall, so a surah is a section fenced off. Others link it to a row of stones in a building, or to a rank, a step up. The Qur'an itself uses the word when it challenges those who doubted it to bring a single surah like it. Every surah but one opens with bismillah. The ninth, al-Tawbah, begins without it. Each has a name, usually taken from a striking word inside it: the Cow, the Bee, the Spider, the Fig. And here's what surprises most first-time readers. The surahs are not arranged in the order they were revealed. After al-Fatiha, they run roughly from longest to shortest. Roughly: there are exceptions, but the pattern is plain. So the earliest revelations, short and urgent, sit mostly at the back, and many of the long later ones sit at the front. Why this order? Most scholars hold that the order of verses within each surah was set by the Prophet ﷺ himself, as Jibril taught him. On the order of the surahs, scholars differ. Many say that too was taught by the Prophet. Others say it was partly arranged by the companions, following what they knew of his recitation. Either way, Muslims read the order as meaningful, not accidental. It means you can open anywhere and begin. It means a child can start at the short end, as you did. And it means the book isn't a timeline. It's more like a house of rooms, each with its own door.
screen: `114 SURAHS, EACH SET APART` · `ALL BUT ONE OPEN WITH BISMILLAH` · `NOT IN THE ORDER REVEALED` · `ROUGHLY LONGEST TO SHORTEST`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open a mushaf, on paper or on your phone. Find the list of surahs, at the back of many Arabic copies, at the front of many English ones. Let your eye run slowly down it: al-Baqarah, Al Imran, an-Nisa, al-Ma'idah, all the way to an-Nas, number one hundred and fourteen. Notice where the ones you know are sitting. If there's no copy near you, picture the line of them, long rooms giving way to small ones. Breathe while you look. The bell holds the time.
Surah. One of the Qur'an's one hundred and fourteen chapters: a section set apart, each with its own name. Today's word.

Your line: longest to shortest. Today, when your list looks long, do the biggest thing while you're fresh and let the day get lighter as it goes. Or start at the short end, the way children do. Either way, start. Day three hundred eleven.

312.title: Verses as signs
312.hook: each verse is an ayah, a sign, like the signs in nature
312.howItsDone: Muslims call each verse of the Qur'an an ayah, a sign, and the Qur'an asks its readers to reflect on the signs in creation as well as on the verses of the book.

segments.voice: Yesterday, surah: one hundred and fourteen of them, running longest to shortest. Your line was longest to shortest. Did you find where the ones you know are sitting? Day three hundred twelve.

A road sign isn't the city. It points to the city. You see it and you know something is out there, ahead of you. Now a sunset. The way your breath keeps going while you sleep. Two strangers who become family. Rain on dry ground. The Qur'an has one word for all of these, and it's the very same word it uses for its own verses. Today: verses as signs.
screen: `A ROAD SIGN ISN'T THE CITY.` → `A SUNSET, A BREATH, THE RAIN.` → `ONE WORD FOR ALL OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Each verse of the Qur'an is called an ayah. The word means a sign, a token, a mark that points past itself. In everyday Arabic, an ayah could be a signal, a landmark, a wonder. The Qur'an uses it for three kinds of things, and it doesn't fence them apart. The verses on the page are ayat. The miracles of the prophets are ayat: Musa's staff, the she-camel of Salih. And the world is full of ayat. In Pickthall's words: "Lo! In the creation of the heavens and the earth and (in) the difference of night and day are tokens (of His sovereignty) for men of understanding." Pickthall says tokens there, but the Arabic is the same word as verses. Surah 30 lists signs one after another, the heavens and the earth, "and the difference of your languages and colours." And another verse, in Pickthall: "We shall show them Our portents on the horizons and within themselves." Portents, tokens, signs: all ayat. So when a Muslim reads a verse, and when a Muslim watches rain come down on dry ground, the Qur'an asks for the same kind of attention. Not only what is this, but what does it point to? How many ayat are there? It depends whom you ask. The early schools of reciters placed a few verse breaks differently, so printed copies don't all give the same total. The words are the same; only the places where one verse ends and the next begins differ. And that's the heart of it. A verse isn't only a sentence to understand. It's a sign to follow, like everything else the Qur'an calls a sign.
screen: `AYAH: A SIGN THAT POINTS PAST ITSELF` · `VERSES, MIRACLES AND THE WORLD` · `ON THE HORIZONS AND WITHIN` · `A VERSE IS FOLLOWED, NOT ONLY READ`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one sign outside. If you can, go to a window or step out the door. If not, close your eyes and listen. Let your attention land on one ordinary thing: a tree, the light on a wall, a bird, the hum of traffic, your own pulse. Don't analyze it. Look at it the way you'd look at a road sign, and ask quietly: what does this point to? Let the question stay open. The bell holds the time.
Ayah. A verse of the Qur'an, and a sign: in one word, the page and the world. Today's word.
Your line: a verse is a sign. Today, notice one thing, in a text or in the world, and treat it like a signpost instead of a wall: ask where it points. Day three hundred twelve.

313.title: Meccan and Medinan
313.hook: early Meccan surahs are short, poetic, about the One and the Day, the later Medinan ones longer and communal
313.howItsDone: Printed copies of the Qur'an usually mark each surah as Meccan or Medinan, and Muslims studying a verse learn which period it comes from to understand what it was answering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ayah: a verse, and a sign. Your line was a verse is a sign. What did you notice that seemed to point somewhere? Day three hundred thirteen.

There's the way you talk when you're trying to wake someone up, and the way you talk when you're helping them set up a new home. The first is short, urgent, vivid: look, listen, get up. The second is longer and practical: here's how we'll share the kitchen, here's what's fair, here's who pays for what. Open the Qur'an near the back, then near the front, and you'll hear something like that difference. Today: Meccan and Medinan.
screen: `WAKING SOMEONE UP.` → `SETTING UP A HOME.` → `THE BACK AND THE FRONT OF THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: The Prophet's mission had two halves. About thirteen years in Mecca, where the Muslims were a small and often persecuted group. Then the hijra, the move to Medina, and about ten years building a community. Scholars sort the surahs by these two periods, and printed copies often say at the top of each surah whether it's Makki or Madani, Meccan or Medinan. Scholars differ on where a handful of surahs belong. The Meccan surahs, mostly toward the back, tend to be short, with a rhythm and rhyme that ring. They speak of the One God, the Day of Judgment, the signs in nature, the prophets who came before. Many open with oaths: by the dawn, by the fig, by time. Think of Surah 112: "Say: He is Allah, the One!" Four lines, and it's done. The Medinan surahs, mostly toward the front, tend to be long. They speak to a community: prayer, fasting and charity, marriage and inheritance, contracts, war and peace, how to live beside neighbors of other faiths. Al-Baqarah is Medinan; its verses on fasting in Ramadan come from Medina. Here's a detail scholars care about. The definition al-Suyuti calls the best known goes by time, not place: before the hijra or after it. So a verse revealed in Mecca years after the hijra, during the farewell pilgrimage, still counts as Medinan. And some surahs hold verses from both periods. Muslims speak of one book here, not two: one voice speaking to one people at two stages of their life: first the heart woken, then the house put in order.
screen: `THIRTEEN YEARS, THEN TEN` · `MECCAN: SHORT, THE ONE AND THE DAY` · `MEDINAN: LONG, A COMMUNITY'S LIFE` · `SORTED BY TIME, NOT PLACE`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: compare Surah 112 with a page of Surah 2. If you have a mushaf or an app, open to al-Ikhlas and read its four lines. Then turn to any page near the start of al-Baqarah and simply look at it. Don't read it all. Feel the difference: a bell's ring, and a long conversation. If you can't open them now, say al-Ikhlas from memory, and picture a full page of close lines beside it. Then rest in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Meccan and Medinan. The two periods of revelation: before the hijra, short and urgent; after it, long and communal. Today's word.
Your line: two cities, one book. Today, notice that you need both voices too: one to wake you up, one to help you run the house. Which one do you need more today? Day three hundred thirteen.

314.title: Thirty parts
314.hook: divided into thirty parts so it can be read in a month
314.howItsDone: Reading one juz' a day in Ramadan is a common practice, and some mosques recite one juz' a night in the tarawih prayer so the whole Qur'an is heard by the end of the month.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Meccan and Medinan: the short surahs that wake the heart, the long ones that put the house in order. Your line was two cities, one book. Which voice did you need more? Day three hundred fourteen.

In Ramadan, in mosques all over the world, something happens night after night. After the evening prayer comes the long night prayer, tarawih, and the imam recites from the Qur'an. In some mosques it's a set amount each night, so that by the end of the month the whole book has been heard, cover to cover. But the book has one hundred and fourteen surahs of wildly different lengths. How do you split it into equal nights? Today: thirty parts.
screen: `RAMADAN, NIGHT AFTER NIGHT.` → `THE WHOLE BOOK IN A MONTH.` → `HOW DO YOU SPLIT IT?`

segments.voice: The Qur'an is divided into thirty parts of roughly equal length. Each is called a juz', which simply means a part, a portion. Thirty fits a month: one juz' a day takes you through the whole book. Each juz' is split again into two halves, each called a hizb, sixty in all, and those into quarters. Open a mushaf and you'll see the markers in the margins. Here's the thing to know: these divisions aren't part of the revelation, and tradition doesn't trace them to the Prophet ﷺ. They were added later, as a reader's aid, by measuring length, not by following meaning. So a juz' can begin in the middle of a surah, even in the middle of a story. The second juz' starts partway through al-Baqarah. Many are known by the words they begin with. And the thirtieth is the one you know. It's usually called Juz' 'Amma, after its first word, 'amma, about what, from the opening of An-Naba': about what are they asking one another? That's the part you walked through in camp four, from An-Naba' to An-Nas. There are older rhythms too. The Prophet advised a companion, Abdullah ibn Amr, to finish the Qur'an in a month. When Abdullah said he could do more, he was told: then in seven days, and not less. From that, some Muslims divide the book into seven portions, one for each day of the week. The thirty parts are the rhythm printed in the margins. Thirty parts, thirty nights, and a whole book in a month.
screen: `THIRTY PARTS OF EQUAL LENGTH` · `A READER'S AID, ADDED LATER` · `JUZ' 'AMMA: THE ONE YOU KNOW` · `A MONTH, OR A WEEK`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: note which juz' you know. Sit, and count on your fingers. Al-Fatiha: that's in the first juz'. Ayat al-Kursi, if you know it: the third. The short surahs from camp four: the thirtieth. If you pray, you can recite one short surah from the thirtieth juz' now, slowly. If you're learning, just say its name and remember the day you met it. The bell holds the time.
Juz'. A part: one of thirty equal portions of the Qur'an, so the whole can be read in a month. Today's word.
Your line: thirty parts, thirty nights. Today, take one big thing you've been putting off and cut it into thirty small pieces. Then do only the first. Day three hundred fourteen.

315.title: The scribes
315.hook: companions wrote verses on palm leaves, bones and parchment, and many memorized it
315.howItsDone: Muslims teach that the Qur'an was both written down by the Prophet's scribes as it was revealed and memorized by many companions, and they still learn it both ways: from the page and by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, juz': thirty parts, so the whole book can be read in a month. Your line was thirty parts, thirty nights. Did you cut one big thing small? Day three hundred fifteen, the end of a week.

Medina, in the Prophet's lifetime. There's no paper mill in town. A new verse has just come to the Prophet ﷺ, and he calls for someone to write it down. What do you reach for? A palm stalk, stripped of its leaves. A thin, flat white stone. The broad shoulder blade of a camel, dried in the sun. A scrap of leather. And while the scribe writes, the people nearby are already saying it over to themselves, fixing it in memory. Today: the scribes.
screen: `NO PAPER MILL IN TOWN.` → `A PALM STALK, A STONE, A BONE.` → `SAYING IT OVER TO THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: The Prophet had a number of companions who wrote the revelation for him; later writers list many of their names. The one who stands out is Zayd ibn Thabit, a young man of Medina who often wrote at the Prophet's side. Years later, describing how he gathered the Qur'an, Zayd named what it had been written on: palm stalks, thin flat stones, and, as he put it, the chests of men. Other reports add shoulder bones and pieces of parchment. So there were always two copies: one scattered on whatever would take ink, and one carried by heart. A story in Bukhari shows both at work. A verse came saying that believers who stay at home are not equal to those who strive in God's cause. The Prophet called for Zayd, with the board and the inkpot and the shoulder bone, and dictated it. Then a blind companion, Ibn Umm Maktum, spoke up: what about someone like me, who can't go? And the verse came again with a few words added: except those who have a disability. Zayd wrote them in. The text answered the man in the room. And the memorizers? The Prophet named four people to learn the Qur'an from: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Salim, Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Others knew large parts by heart. Now look back at this week. The name, Qur'an: recitation. Twenty-three years of it arriving. One hundred and fourteen surahs. Each verse an ayah, a sign. Meccan and Medinan. Thirty parts. And now the people who held it, on bone and in the heart.
screen: `ZAYD AT THE PROPHET'S SIDE` · `PALM STALKS, STONES AND BONES` · `A VERSE ANSWERS A BLIND MAN` · `FOUR TO LEARN IT FROM`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one verse on paper. Take a pen and any scrap: an envelope, a receipt, the corner of a notebook. Write one verse you know, in Arabic if you can, in English if not, or just its first words. Write slowly, as if ink were rare. Then put the pen down, close your eyes, and say it once from memory. Two copies: one on the page, one in you. The bell holds the time.
The scribes. The companions who wrote the Qur'an down as it came, on palm stalks, stones and bone, while others kept it by heart. Today's word.
Your line: on bone and heart. Today, keep the verse you wrote somewhere you'll see it, a pocket, a mirror, a phone case, and say it once more before you sleep. Day three hundred fifteen.
